claim: India's national ambient standard for PM2.5 is 40 µg/m³ as an annual mean and 60 µg/m³ as a 24-hour value; for PM10 it is 60 and 100 µg/m³.

The Indian annual standard is an arithmetic mean of at least 104 measurements a year at a site; the standard requires 24-hour values to be met 98% of the time and not exceeded on two consecutive monitoring days.

WHO's 2021 guideline levels for PM2.5 are 5 µg/m³ annual mean and 15 µg/m³ 24-hour (99th percentile), with interim targets of 35/25/15/10 (annual) and 75/50/37.5/25 (24-hour); the guidelines are not legally binding.
notes: Table values via AirClim reproduction; non-binding status via WHO Q&A

claim: India's annual PM2.5 standard (40 µg/m³) is eight times the WHO 2021 guideline level (5 µg/m³); at 40 µg/m³ it is less stringent than even WHO interim target 1 (35 µg/m³).
notes: arithmetic comparison of two sourced values

claim: WHO estimates ambient air pollution caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019, 89% of them in low- and middle-income countries; 68% were from ischaemic heart disease and stroke.
India's AQI has six categories: Good 0-50, Satisfactory 51-100, Moderate 101-200, Poor 201-300, Very Poor 301-400, Severe 401-500.

The AQI is generated hourly from sub-indices for eight pollutants (PM2.5, PM10, CO, NO2, SO2, NH3, O3, lead); the highest sub-index is reported as the AQI, using a running average of the preceding 24 hours (8 hours for CO and ozone) with at least 16 hours of data required.
notes: Phase 2: confirm against CPCB 2014 NAQI report

claim: CPCB acknowledged in November 2026 that hourly particulate readings above 999 µg/m³ are excluded from AQI calculation because the 2015 validation method assumed analysers calibrated to 0-1,000 µg/m³; such hours appear as data gaps and do not count toward the 24-hour average.

Reports at the time said 45 of Delhi's 59 monitoring stations had missing hourly readings for at least one pollutant during the episode; ministry sources said the methodology was under internal review with no external expert group constituted.
notes: Unnamed sources; treat as reported, not verified

claim: The AQI is capped at 500; CPCB states values above this remain 'Severe' and extrapolation would not change the health category. A capped index therefore cannot distinguish 500 from much higher concentrations.
notes: second sentence is analytical inference

claim: As of March 2026 India's ambient monitoring network had 1,646 stations (manual and real-time) across 603 cities in 28 states and 7 union territories; SAMEER shows near real-time AQI for more than 292 cities.
NCAP, launched in 2019, covers 130 cities; ₹16,423.55 crore in performance-linked grants was released FY2019-20 to FY2025-26 and cities report using ₹11,575.54 crore (70.5%).

Government reports that in FY2025-26, 108 of 130 NCAP cities had lower annual PM10 than in 2017-18; 72 by more than 20%, 26 by more than 40%, and 14 met the national standard. NCAP targets are framed on PM10, not PM2.5.
notes: Official self-report, not independent evaluation

claim: NCAP source-apportionment studies attribute about 40-50% of PM10 in most cities to construction and road dust, according to government.
notes: Applies to PM10, not PM2.5; city-specific shares vary

claim: CAQM directed that only BS-VI, CNG or electric buses may enter Delhi from 1 November 2026, and set a revised industrial PM emission norm of 50 mg/Nm³ for polluting and large industries from 1 October 2026.

GBD 2019 attributes 1.67 million deaths in India in 2019 (95% UI 1.42-1.92) to air pollution, 17.8% of all deaths: 0.98 million to ambient particulate matter and 0.61 million to household air pollution.
Between 1990 and 2019 the death rate attributed to household air pollution fell 64.2% while that attributed to ambient particulate matter rose 115.3% (UI 28.3-344.4).

GBD 2019 values lost output from air-pollution deaths and illness at US$36.8 billion (UI 27.4-47.7) in 2019, 1.36% of GDP; as a share of state GDP the loss was highest in low-income states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh), while Delhi had the highest per-capita loss.
notes: Cost-of-illness method: national output loss, not household income loss

claim: A 2024 difference-in-differences study using district civil-registration deaths 2009-2019 found each 10 µg/m³ increase in annual PM2.5 associated with 8.6% (95% CI 6.4-10.8) higher annual mortality; it argues GBD exposure-response functions drawn from low-pollution countries may be inappropriate for India.

The same study estimates 3.8 million deaths (2.9-4.9) over 2009-2019 attributable to PM2.5 above the Indian standard, and 16.6 million (13.0-21.8) above the WHO guideline; the counterfactual chosen changes the estimate more than fourfold.
notes: Illustrates counterfactual dependence of attributable-death estimates

claim: Population-weighted annual PM2.5 in India was 41 µg/m³ in 2023 on AQLI's satellite-derived data, up from 2022; all 1.4 billion people live above the WHO guideline and 46% above the national annual standard.
Estimates of the share of Indians living above the national standard differ by source and period: 46% (AQLI, 2023 satellite data) versus 81.9% (de Bont et al., 2009-2019 modelled data).
notes: Different years, models and spatial methods; not a trend

claim: AQLI estimates that meeting the WHO guideline would add 3.5 years to average Indian life expectancy, 5 years for 544.4 million Northern Plains residents, and 8.2 years for Delhi residents.
notes: Model output with specific counterfactual (WHO guideline, permanent reduction)

claim: AQLI reports that pollution in districts with NCAP non-attainment cities was 10.5% lower in 2023 than 2017; the revised NCAP target is a 40% reduction by 2026 for 131 cities.
notes: Government sources cite 130 cities and PM10; AQLI uses satellite PM2.5

claim: In TERI-ARAI receptor modelling for Delhi and NCR towns, dust contributed 31-34% of PM2.5 in summer but about 15% in winter; biomass burning 22% in winter vs 15% in summer; secondary ions 26% in winter vs 17-18% in summer; vehicles 20-23% in winter vs 18-20% in summer; industry 10-13% in both.
TERI-ARAI measured average winter PM2.5 of 168 ± 45 µg/m³ across its Delhi-NCR sampling sites (range 92-254).

IIT Kanpur's 2016 study for DPCC found secondary particles (nitrate, sulphate, ammonium) to be the most important single component of winter PM2.5 at its Delhi sites, with average winter PM2.5 of about 375 µg/m³ at sampling sites.
notes: Sampling-site averages, not city-wide annual means

claim: Transport's share of Delhi's PM2.5 emission inventory is put at 20% (IIT Kanpur 2015), 39% (TERI-ARAI 2018) and 41% (SAFAR-IITM 2018): emission inventories and ambient apportionment measure different things and are not interchangeable.
notes: Phase 2: confirm each figure in the original reports

claim: CSE's analysis of Decision Support System outputs for 10-20 November found Delhi's local sources contributed about 35% of PM2.5 in 2025 (27.3% in 2024) and surrounding NCR districts about 25.8% (36% in 2023); vehicles were 51-53% of the local share across 2023-25.
notes: Model-based (DSS), episode window only; not annual shares

claim: CSE reports Delhi had received ₹81.36 crore under NCAP by December 2025 but utilised only ₹14.1 crore (17%).
notes: Phase 2: verify against PRANA portal

claim: Real-time measurements inside Delhi auto-rickshaws (about 180 hours) found trip-averaged PM2.5 geometric mean of 190 µg/m³, 1.5 times simultaneous ambient levels; black carbon was 3.6 times and ultrafine particle number 8.4 times ambient.

On-road and near-road emissions accounted for 30% of in-vehicle PM2.5 but 68% of black carbon and 86% of ultrafine particles in auto-rickshaws: fixed ambient monitors understate exposure of people who work in traffic, especially for combustion particles.
notes: second clause is an inference from the measured ratios

claim: An Airvoice analysis of official datasets up to 2025 found about 40% of India's districts have no government-operated monitoring station, about half of continuous stations deliver stable data, and station numbers correlate only moderately with PM2.5 levels.
notes: Commercial author; definitions differ from CSE

claim: CSE's 2026 State of India's Environment report estimates only about 15% of India's population (about 200 million) lives within 10 km of a continuous monitor.
notes: Secondary report; original not yet read

claim: An unmonitored district is not a low-exposure district: monitoring is concentrated in large metros, and several highly populated districts in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh are poorly monitored or outside the real-time network.
notes: First clause is the brief's analytic rule; evidence clause from report

claim: PMUY connections rose sharply after 2016, but in 2021-22 9.6% of beneficiaries took no refill, 11.3% one refill and 56.5% four or fewer, against about seven refills a year needed for exclusive cooking use.
notes: Reported figures; Phase 2: trace to PPAC/RTI source

claim: Research in Delhi and Jharkhand reported by Mongabay found refill cost, access, misconceptions and women's limited decision-making autonomy constrain consistent LPG use among PMUY households.

Under GRAP, construction is restricted as AQI rises and fully banned at Stage 4 (AQI above 450); the Supreme Court's 24 November 2021 order required financial assistance to workers affected by construction bans, paid from labour-cess (BOCW welfare) funds.

The Supreme Court later directed that whenever GRAP closes construction, affected workers are to be compensated even without a specific court order; it declined a plea to let non-polluting construction trades continue during Stages 3 and 4.

Delhi announced ₹8,000 for registered construction workers after the November 2024 GRAP-4 closure and ₹10,000 after 16 days of GRAP-III in December 2025; eligibility was limited to workers registered and verified with the Delhi BOCW Welfare Board.

Welfare Board dashboard figures cited in December 2024 showed 1,378,199 workers ever registered but only 89,518 active members; 1,288,681 memberships had expired and 507,863 of 716,174 renewal applications had been approved.
notes: Second-hand dashboard figures via an advocate's affidavit; Phase 2: check dashboard

claim: In a rapid survey of 75 workers at four central-Delhi sites (filed in a December 2024 affidavit), only five were registered with the Welfare Board and none had received the ₹8,000 payment.
notes: Small convenience sample; illustrative, not representative

claim: In November 2026 the Welfare Board said about one lakh workers had been paid (nearly ₹100 crore) while its website listed about 2.15 lakh registered workers; a union affidavit says about 1,700 workers still await payment.
notes: Figures from different points in time and definitions do not reconcile

claim: Compensation is tied to registration, so the registration gap determines who is protected: unregistered and migrant workers whose registrations have lapsed lose wages during restrictions without receiving relief.
notes: Analytical inference from C-claims on registration and payment

claim: In a Bengaluru garment factory, hourly output fell with fine particulate pollution; effects were heterogeneous across workers and tasks, and attentive managers mitigated losses by reassigning workers.
notes: Output/efficiency effect within formal employment; not a wage or household-income effect

claim: In a September 2025 survey of 582 Delhi households, 9 in 10 affluent households had air conditioners versus fewer than 1 in 10 low-income households; the authors report air purifiers are mostly owned by the rich.
The same survey found household spending rose during pollution months, dominated by medical expenses; coughing, breathing difficulty and eye irritation were the most reported symptoms.
notes: Self-reported; magnitudes shown only in figures

claim: Workplace exposure to outdoor air was higher the lower a respondent's class, and a large majority across all classes reported not using masks during severe pollution.
notes: Self-reported

claim: In a Tamil Nadu rural-urban cohort of 1,285 pregnant women with directly measured household PM2.5 in each trimester, a 10 µg/m³ increase was associated with 4 g lower birthweight (95% CI 1.08-6.76) and 2% higher odds of low birthweight.

Analyses of NFHS-5 (2019-21) linked to satellite PM2.5 associate higher in-utero exposure with low birthweight and preterm birth: one reports a 5% higher LBW prevalence and 12% higher preterm prevalence per 10 µg/m³, with steeper risk above about 40 µg/m³ and greater susceptibility in northern districts.

A second NFHS-5 analysis of 208,181 children (mean in-utero PM2.5 56 µg/m³) found 52% higher odds of preterm birth in the highest versus lowest exposure octile (AOR 1.52, 1.43-1.61) but only a small LBW difference (AOR 1.06).
notes: Effect sizes differ across studies using the same survey; cross-sectional design

claim: Using national survey data, each 10 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 was associated with 10% higher anaemia, 11% higher acute respiratory infection and 5% higher low-birthweight prevalence among Indian children; nitrate, elemental carbon and ammonium were more strongly associated than total mass.
notes: Observational; suggests PM2.5 mass may understate harm from combustion species

claim: A ten-city time-series study (2008-2019) found a 10 µg/m³ rise in 2-day average PM2.5 associated with 1.4% higher daily mortality (0.7-2.2); associations persisted below the Indian 24-hour standard of 60 µg/m³.
geography: Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, Pune, Shimla, Varanasi

claim: Under GRAP Stages III-IV, physical classes are discontinued for children up to Class V and higher classes move to hybrid mode; CEEW's review of Directorate of Education circulars found closures in some years lasted up to 15 days, often announced with less than a day's notice.

CEEW argues online classes give limited continuity because of digital access gaps and reduced peer interaction; students it interviewed (about 30, Classes V and X, one school) all preferred attending school.
notes: Small qualitative sample; advocacy for in-school alternatives (masking, planning, purifiers)

claim: A 2012 CPCB-commissioned study reported lung-function deficits in 43.5% of Delhi schoolchildren versus 25.7% in a control group.
notes: Source unreachable; cannot be rated above Limited until read

claim: Indian evidence linking air pollution to children's cognition is preliminary: the most-cited result (Odisha, IQ 80 vs 98 between high- and low-pollution sites) is a conference abstract without established peer review.
notes: Health Policy Watch confirms the result was presented at the World Conference on Lung Health and published in its abstract book; peer review not established

claim: An IIT Kanpur network of 538 low-cost sensor nodes across every block of Bihar's 38 districts found rural air violated national standards on nearly 90% of days, with winter PM2.5 in northwest Bihar routinely around 210 µg/m³.
notes: Low-cost sensors; BSPCB chair says they are about 60% accurate; IIT Kanpur cites co-location trials

claim: The AMRIT study attributes rural Bihar's pollution mainly to household solid biomass, seasonal stubble burning, dust and brick kilns; Bihar's kiln owners' association says most kilns have converted to zigzag technology under a March 2022 BSPCB notification.
notes: Contested attributions; sensor data cannot apportion sources

claim: The IIT Kanpur lead investigator estimates Bihar has roughly one regulatory monitor per 3.5-4 million people, concentrated in urban centres.
notes: Stakeholder estimate

claim: In Patna, receptor modelling found dust the largest PM10 source in winter (30%) and summer (57%); secondary inorganic particles 24% (winter) vs 9% (summer); dispersion modelling put the residential sector at 28% of PM2.5 in winter and 6% in summer, transport 21-23%, and sources outside the city 46% in summer and 16% in winter.

Annual PM10 averages of 166.75 and 159.67 µg/m³ were recorded at NAMP stations at Anpara and Renusagar (Sonbhadra, Singrauli region) for April 2023 to May 2024, against a 60 µg/m³ standard; PM2.5 was not reported at these stations.

Applicants before the NGT (OA 240/2024) allege 359 industries including thermal power plants and coal mines, health harm and heavy-metal contamination; official health data supplied by the district CMO recorded few lung-disease patients at local health centres, illustrating weak health surveillance rather than absence of harm.
notes: Second clause is inference; allegations unadjudicated

claim: Black carbon concentrations above 200 µg/m³ were measured close to Singrauli's coal-fired power plants in a 2013 campaign; satellite NO2 shows a persistent hotspot over its seven plants.
notes: Abstract read in Phase 2

claim: Mumbai's 2023 NEERI study found resuspended road dust (linked to Metro and real-estate construction) the main PM10 source; for PM2.5, secondary aerosols (22%) and marine sources (26%) made up 48%.

Mumbai's receptor modelling attributed 12-20% of PM to industry while the inventory-based dispersion model gave under 1%, because small informal units such as 'bhatties' were missing from the inventory: inventories systematically miss informal sources.
notes: Last clause generalises; supported here, check elsewhere

claim: CAQM reported 5,114 farm fires in Punjab and 662 in Haryana between 15 September and 30 November 2025, down 53% on 2024 and 93% (Punjab) on 2021; it credits machinery, enforcement, ex-situ straw use and district plans.
notes: Satellite fire counts can miss small or late-day fires; Phase 2: check for critiques

claim: In six Patiala villages (3,644 participants, 2018-19), lung function fell during crop-residue burning periods (mean PM2.5 increase 167 µg/m³): FEV1 declined 16% in boys and 26% in girls aged 10-18, with smaller declines in adults.
notes: Cross-sectional, purposive sample; abstract

claim: Zigzag kilns cut coal use about 20% and black carbon and PM about 75% compared with fixed-chimney kilns, produce about 8 bricks per kg of coal versus 5, and cost about ₹40 lakh to retrofit with a reported one- to two-year payback.
notes: Figures cited from other studies by WRI; Phase 2: trace to performance assessment

claim: Each Bihar kiln employs 120-150 workers, mostly trained on the job; owners report converted kilns cannot reach full efficiency without trained workers, and workers live for months in temporary housing exposed to coal dust and heat.

Anti-Slavery International's Punjab kiln survey found 96% of moulders had taken advances, wages were withheld for whole 8-10-month seasons, families were paid as units through the male head, and 65-80% of children under 14 worked in summer months.
notes: Advocacy organisation; older data

claim: NSS-based analysis finds 47% of migrants working in brick kilns are Scheduled Castes and about 16% Scheduled Tribes, against 18.8% and 7.7% of the all-sector migrant workforce.
notes: Data year to confirm in Phase 2

claim: There are over one lakh brick kilns in India producing about 250 billion bricks a year.
notes: Industry/expert estimates, no official count

claim: A two-year cluster-randomised trial in 180 classes (about 9,000 students) in Delhi's Kendriya Vidyalaya schools, winters 2024-25 and 2025-26, found an air-pollution education campaign raised awareness and protective behaviour, reduced self-reported breathing difficulty and marginally improved working memory, mainly in year one.

In the same trial HEPA purifiers significantly reduced classroom PM2.5, but the purifier-plus-education arm underperformed education alone on working memory (year one) and spirometry (year two); students in purifier classrooms reduced protective behaviour outside school, consistent with a moral-hazard offset.
notes: Policy brief only; full effect sizes not yet available

claim: Education effects spread to untreated classrooms through peer networks; behavioural effects attenuated in year two as controls caught up.

IIT Bombay's evaluation of the Connaught Place smog tower found PM reductions of 48-56% within 20 m, 30-34% at 21-99 m and 12-13% at 109-199 m; DPCC told the NGT in November 2023 that the towers were ineffective and not justified.

DPCC's affidavit put tower capital cost at about ₹25 crore each and operation at about ₹15 lakh per month, and stated the Anand Vihar tower was non-operational with no measurable effect at a monitor 30 m away.
notes: Phase 2: confirm against the affidavit text

claim: Government stated in 2021 that early smog-tower results showed an 80% reduction; later independent evaluation found effects confined to a few hundred metres, illustrating the gap between launch claims and measured performance.
notes: 80% claim now sourced (Deccan Herald, 1 Oct 2021); comparison with IIT-B results is derived

claim: CEEW finds limited evidence on anti-smog gun effectiveness; deploying 250-600 guns on large Delhi buildings would cost about ₹5-12 crore plus electricity and need 25-90 lakh litres of water a day, while covering under 0.5% of Delhi's area.
Delhi's 2026 action plan expands anti-smog guns and water sprinklers at large scale while experts question enforcement capacity and the evidence for these measures.

In Chintan's 2023 Delhi study, abnormal lung function was found in 86% of sanitation workers (safai karamcharis) and security guards and 75% of waste pickers, versus 45% of an indoor office-worker control group; 27% of sanitation workers, 17% of waste pickers and 10% of guards had severe impairment, none in controls.
notes: Cross-sectional; control group differs in other ways (income, occupation); association not causation

claim: Over 60% of sanitation workers, 50% of waste pickers and 30% of security guards did not know about protective equipment; nearly half of waste pickers burned wood or coal to keep warm in winter and over 30% burned waste.
Women in all three occupational groups had lower lung function than men in Chintan's study.

Properly fitted masks reduce exposure, but mask use in Delhi has been low; researchers attribute this to low awareness and social norms, and questioned what a mass distribution of 5 million masks would achieve.
Work-from-home advisories issued during severe pollution do not reach daily-wage workers, vendors, construction labourers and delivery staff, for whom staying home means losing income.
notes: Illustrative testimony plus survey context

claim: A Health Ministry advisory of November 2024 asks states to scale up sentinel surveillance of air-pollution-related disease under the National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health and to expand sentinel hospital networks; it names children, pregnant women, the elderly, people with pre-existing conditions and at-risk occupations as vulnerable.
notes: Letter read in Phase 2; the 2017 start date of surveillance from search snippets was not confirmed and has been removed

claim: Clean Air Fund grants supported Mahila Housing Trust and Help Delhi Breathe to train more than 75 women construction workers in three Delhi resettlement colonies (Bakkarwala, Gokulpuri, Sawda Ghevra) to use AQI devices and engage local authorities; five became peer trainers.
notes: Outputs reported by funder; no independent outcome evaluation found

claim: Clean Air Fund reports that 94% of women construction workers it surveyed avoid talking about air pollution for fear of losing their jobs, and that construction bans in peak months stopped women from earning.
notes: Survey details not given

claim: Clean Air Fund funds Health Care Without Harm to build a network of health workers as clean-air advocates, including work with about 100 hospitals in polluted regions to monitor air quality and communicate risks to patients.
notes: Activity/output claims

claim: The World Bank approved about $299.66 million for Uttar Pradesh and $300 million for Haryana clean-air programmes in December 2025, described as the first airshed-based multi-sector state programmes; UP's includes clean cooking for 3.9 million households and 15,000 electric three-wheelers.

Delhi's homeless-shelter board (DUSIB) runs about 197 shelters with capacity for 7,092 people, expanding to over 11,000 with 400 winter tents from 15 November 2026 to 15 March 2027; the plan lists bedding, water, toilets and power but no air filtration.
notes: Last clause: absence in the reported plan, not confirmed in the plan itself

claim: NCAP allocated ₹3,072 crore FY2019-20 to FY2025-26 and a further ₹16,539 crore went to 48 million-plus cities through the 15th Finance Commission challenge fund; ₹3,623 crore was released for crop-residue management in Punjab, Haryana, UP and Delhi FY2018-19 to FY2024-25.
notes: Compiled from Parliament answers; Phase 2: verify

claim: External finance includes World Bank loans for UP (about ₹2,741 crore) and Haryana (about ₹2,498 crore), UNDP projects (about ₹90 crore, 2023-25), UNEP (about ₹53 crore) and Swiss SDC (about ₹72 crore, 2019-23, plus about ₹90 crore for IGP transboundary work).
notes: Compiled figures; Phase 2: verify each

claim: International funding for ground-level ozone was about $111 million in 2024, 0.4% of total air quality funding tracked.

In the HAPIN randomised trial (3,200 pregnant women; sites included Tamil Nadu), free LPG stoves and fuel achieved near-complete uptake and cut median personal PM2.5 from 70.7 to 23.9 µg/m³, yet birth weight did not differ significantly (adjusted difference 19.6 g, 95% CI -10.1 to 49.2).

HAPIN follow-up analyses report no reduction in infant stunting and no clear effect on childhood lung function outcomes; even with LPG, personal exposure remained well above the WHO guideline, so partial exposure reduction may be insufficient for some outcomes.
notes: Second clause is interpretation; does not imply clean cooking lacks other benefits (time, burns, ambient emissions)

claim: Direct evidence that community clean-air shelters reduce health harm is limited and inconclusive; most evidence concerns indoor filtration performance rather than use or outcomes, and no studies of uptake by those most at risk were found.
notes: UW DEOHS page read in Phase 2: researchers say evidence on shelter effectiveness is inconclusive; a literature review found little evidence

claim: Thirty food-delivery riders measured in Ghaziabad in December 2020 had breathing-zone exposures of 516 µg/m³ PM10 and 180 µg/m³ PM2.5 while riding, with benzene of 19 µg/m³ against a 5 µg/m³ national standard; 67% were unaware of health risks, and traffic junctions drove modelled risk.
notes: Small preliminary study; reported second-hand

claim: In December 2025, with GRAP-IV in force, a gig workers' association said platform workers were working long hours outdoors without pollution allowance, health cover or protective gear and demanded a per-order 'pollution surcharge' on high-AQI days; a parliamentary standing committee had recommended that companies give delivery riders free N95 masks and company-funded annual health check-ups.
notes: Replaces Phase 1 wording (lost incentives and penalties for logging off), which the cited source did not support

claim: Of ₹87,478 crore collected nationally as construction workers' welfare cess up to November 2022, ₹49,269 crore (56%) had been spent and ₹38,209 crore (44%) remained unutilised, according to a reply in Parliament.
notes: Most recent national figure found; Phase 2: look for 2024-25 replies

claim: Worker federations attribute low disbursement partly to welfare boards' weak enrolment and registration of workers.

The Code on Social Security came into force on 21 November 2025, defining gig and platform workers and requiring aggregators to contribute 1-2% of annual turnover (capped at 5% of payments to workers) to a social security fund whose benefit framework was still being finalised.
notes: Effective date confirmed by PIB release

claim: The other three labour codes do not extend minimum earnings, employment protection or working-condition guarantees to gig and platform workers.
Dispersion modelling for Patna attributed about 11% of winter PM10 and 10% of winter PM2.5 to industry and brick kilns within and outside the city.

From 2024-25 waste pickers were added to the NAMASTE scheme (Ministry of Social Justice), which offers enumeration, occupational safety training, PPE kits, occupation-based ID cards and Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY health insurance.

The 2016 Solid Waste Management Rules required municipalities to recognise and issue ID cards to waste pickers, but most urban local bodies had not issued cards, because of budget constraints or reluctance, according to the waste pickers' federation.
notes: Advocacy source; city-level compliance not verified

claim: NAMASTE coverage figures vary by date and definition; by August 2025 the Ministry reported 85,819 sewer and septic tank workers digitally profiled and 76,736 given PPE kits. Waste-picker coverage figures were not found in an official source.
notes: Corrected in Phase 2 to the figures in the cited report; earlier 2.8 lakh waste-picker figure dropped (no retrievable source)

claim: The OSH Code came into force on 21 November 2025; government states every employee is eligible for a free annual health check-up and that the Code applies with a uniform threshold of 10 employees, or to any establishment with even one employee in hazardous work.
notes: Effective date from PIB release; health check-up and threshold from OSH backgrounder

claim: The OSH Code creates duties for employers of wage workers (including contract and migrant workers) but self-employed waste pickers and vendors have no employer to whom these duties attach; their protection runs through schemes such as NAMASTE instead.
notes: Analytical inference

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Bangladesh averaged 60.8 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #1 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 5.5 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Nepal averaged 38.3 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #4 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 3.3 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Madhesh, Koshi, Lumbini.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Pakistan averaged 39.0 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #3 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 3.3 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Islamabad, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Indonesia averaged 18.6 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #51 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 1.3 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Jakarta, North Sumatra, Banten.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Thailand averaged 23.1 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #32 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 1.8 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Chiang Rai, Phayao, Nan.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Vietnam averaged 25.6 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #22 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 2 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Hanoi, Phu Tho, Vinh Phuc.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Philippines averaged 17.1 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #57 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 1.2 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Benguet, Metro Manila, Rizal.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: On AQLI's satellite-derived estimates, population-weighted PM2.5 in Cambodia averaged 18.8 µg/m³ in 2023 (ranked #48 most polluted country), shortening average life expectancy by 1.4 years relative to the WHO guideline; the most polluted subnational areas were Phnom Penh, Banteay Meanchey, Kandal.
notes: Same method and year for all eight countries; not a ground-monitor measurement

claim: The World Bank states air pollution caused over 159,000 premature deaths and 2.5 billion days of illness in Bangladesh in 2019, with estimated health costs equal to 8.3% of GDP.

The World Bank approved the US$290 million Bangladesh Clean Air Project on 18 June 2025; it plans to strengthen the Department of Environment's monitoring network, operationalise continuous emissions monitoring of major industrial sources, build five vehicle inspection centres and upgrade two, deploy 20 mobile testing units, and introduce 400 electric buses replacing diesel buses under a single-operator-per-franchise model.
notes: Approved objectives, not results; instrument split (credit/grant) not stated in release

claim: The World Bank approved a US$52 million credit for the Nepal Clean Air and Prosperity Project on 11 March 2026, complemented by a US$5 million grant from the Resilient Asia Program funded by the UK FCDO and Swiss SDC; it aims to help about 400 enterprises adopt electric or modern biomass boilers/furnaces or emission controls, focusing on Kathmandu Valley, the Terai and foothills, implemented by Nepal's Departments of Industry and Environment.
notes: Approved targets, not results

claim: The World Bank approved a US$300 million IDA loan for the Punjab Clean Air Program on 28 March 2025, supporting Punjab's Smog Mitigation Action Plan with 5,000 super seeders, 600 electric buses, more regulatory-grade monitors and two fuel-testing laboratories; it states an aim to cut PM2.5 in Lahore Division (13 million people) by 35% over a decade.
notes: Target, not a measured result

claim: The World Bank describes the Indo-Gangetic Plains and Himalayan Foothills (IGP-HF) as the world's most polluted airshed and lists dedicated clean-air operations in Pakistan (Punjab), Bangladesh, India (Uttar Pradesh and Haryana) and Nepal (anticipated 2026); the UK contributes through the Climate Action for a Resilient Asia programme.

The World Bank's 2025 regional report says nearly one billion people in the IGP-HF breathe unhealthy air, around one million die prematurely each year, and economic losses are close to 10% of regional GDP annually.
notes: Modelled estimates from press summary

claim: The World Bank's Striving for Clean Air finds that PM2.5 at any South Asian location originates from upwind sources extending over several hundred kilometres, and concludes that effective management requires coordination across sectors and upwind regions.

In Striving for Clean Air's most cost-effective scenario (each state or province cutting exposure below the next WHO interim target), mean South Asian exposure falls to 30 µg/m³, 40% below 2018, at about US$5.7 billion a year (0.11% of GDP) to 2030, about half for household-sector measures.

The World Bank's Towards Clean Air in Nepal (2025) reports air pollution as Nepal's number one risk factor for death and disability, reducing average life expectancy by 3.4 years, causing about 26,000 premature deaths a year and costing over 6% of GDP; the Kathmandu Valley and Terai are hotspots with no significant improvement over a decade, and transboundary airflows carry pollutants across borders.
notes: Life-expectancy figure differs from AQLI's 3.3 years: different models

claim: The World Bank frames its India clean-air support around the Indo-Gangetic Plain airshed (Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal), including US$300 million for Haryana and nearly 200 new monitors linked to a decision-support system.

ADB's technical assistance TA 10537-REG (project 58076-001, active; TA report April 2025) supports its Asia Clean Blue Skies Program across countries including Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam, with listed sources of US$630,000 and US$1.0 million from the Technical Assistance Special Fund, US$1.0 million from the Japan Fund for the Joint Crediting Mechanism and US$1.5 million from the Urban Resilience Trust Fund.
notes: Listed sources summed would be US$4.13m; the page does not state a total

claim: ADB's March 2026 report assesses air quality, monitoring capacity, emission sources, governance and financing across eight ASEAN cities, prepared with support from the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility.

Clean Air Fund reports a 2023 study estimating that air pollution potentially caused more than 10,000 deaths and over 5,000 hospitalisations a year in Jakarta, with an economic burden of about US$2.9 billion (2.2% of the capital's gross regional product).
notes: Second-hand report of a modelled study

claim: Clean Air Fund began programming in Indonesia in 2025; Jakarta is one of 14 Breathe Cities (with C40 Cities and Bloomberg Philanthropies), and with Clean Air Fund support Vital Strategies worked with the Jakarta Environment Agency on using local health and economic data to prioritise clean-air action.
notes: Grant amounts not stated

claim: A Vital Strategies and ITB source-apportionment study at three Jakarta sites found gasoline and diesel vehicles contributed 32-41% of PM2.5 in the wet season and 42-57% in the dry season; coal combustion reached 14% and open burning 9% at the eastern site; secondary inorganic aerosol was 1-16%.
notes: Unclear how much vehicle share is on-road vs off-road; three urban background sites

claim: Clean Air Fund funded community-led monitoring in the Philippines and Indonesia (among five countries) in 2022-2024; a GAIA project equipped 34 volunteers in the Philippines, Nigeria and Indonesia with wearable monitors and found WHO guidelines exceeded on 85-100% of days, while WALHI supported volunteers in Surabaya near the Benowo waste-to-energy plant.
notes: Funder account; volunteer wearable data, not regulatory monitoring

claim: CCAC lists a 2026 project in Cambodia to scale up integrated rice-straw management to reduce black carbon, implemented by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), responding to a request from Cambodia's Ministry of Environment.
notes: Project page blocked (403); budget not found

claim: Thailand's science ministry (MHESI) launched 'Zero Burn to Earn' in 2026 to pay farmers for crop residue instead of burning it in eight northern provinces; it reports eight pilot routes processed 330,000 kg of residue in four months and signed one-year agreements with five firms to buy 40,000 tonnes a year (over 30 million baht).
notes: Self-reported pilot figures; the claimed PM2.5 reduction (270 kg) is a ministry estimate, not a measured air-quality change

claim: Viet Nam's National Action Plan on Air Pollution Control 2026-2030 targets a 20% cut in Hanoi's annual average PM2.5 by 2030 compared with 2024 and at least 80% of days rated good or moderate, according to WHO and UNDP.
notes: Plan targets, not achieved results

claim: The E-Mobility ASAP project in the Philippines is reported as GEF-funded, implemented by the Department of Trade and Industry and Board of Investments with UNIDO, with Clean Air Asia as executing consortium lead, running to June 2027.
notes: Primary pages blocked; budget unconfirmed

claim: Wellcome awarded the PREDICT-ASIA research grant in 2025 to study combined effects of air pollution and heat on health in Asia, with grantholders at Nanyang Technological University (Singapore) and Chiang Mai University among others.
notes: Research grant; not evidence of health improvement

claim: Clean Air Fund and IGES's November 2026 report estimates ambient air pollution causes at least 300,000 deaths a year in Southeast Asia and that delayed action can cost 1-2% of GDP in key countries.

Clean Air Fund and CPI's 2026 funding report covers international development funding 2020-2024: US$124.6 billion was committed as total air-quality-related funding, but under 1% of international development funding went to projects with outdoor air quality as an explicit objective.
notes: Different denominator and period from the philanthropic report; never combine

claim: Clean Air Fund's 2026 philanthropic analysis (2019-2023 data) reports foundation funding for air quality more than doubled between 2019 and 2023, grew about 2% from 2022 to 2023, and states $478 million was spent on air-quality projects, under 0.1% of global philanthropic giving.
notes: The page does not say whether $478m is a single year or the five-year total

claim: Clean Air Fund states its sustained work with national and state governments helped unlock US$600 million in World Bank clean-air financing for Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.
notes: Self-reported contribution claim; the World Bank amounts are separate public finance, not Clean Air Fund money

claim: Clean Air Fund names IIT Kanpur as a partner whose ATMAN Centre of Excellence established a low-cost sensor network across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

State of Global Air 2025 (2023 data) reports almost 2.6 billion people exposed to household air pollution from solid cooking fuels, and that 95% of air-pollution-attributable deaths in adults over 60 are from noncommunicable diseases.
State of Global Air reports that in 2021 one in three deaths in Central, Southeast and South Asia was linked to air pollution, and that major sources vary across the three regions.

WHO's 2026 technical brief puts air pollution at about 6.6 million deaths a year globally, close to 84% from noncommunicable diseases, and names children, pregnant women, older people, people with chronic disease and the lowest socioeconomic groups as most at risk.

Modelling of brick-kiln clusters north of Dhaka (published 2013) attributed about 40% of measured fine PM to brick kilns during the October-March firing season, while transport dominates within the city.
notes: Older study; source shares change over time

claim: Lahore's 2023 emissions inventory (2020-21 data) attributes about 35% of PM2.5 emissions to transport, 33% to crop-residue burning, 29% to waste burning and 3% to industry; the widely quoted 83% transport figure refers to all pollutants by weight, dominated by carbon monoxide.
notes: Inventory reported second-hand; inventories measure emissions, not what people breathe

claim: Punjab's real-time air quality portal launched on 1 October 2025 with 30 regulatory-grade stations and has expanded to 59.

In a 2022 cross-sectional study of 228 Delhi outdoor workers (auto drivers, vendors, sweepers; lung tests on 63), most reported that air quality severely affected their health and many had restricted lung function, but impairment was statistically associated with smoking and age rather than with measured pollution.
notes: Perception-based; no personal exposure measurement

claim: A 2026 cross-sectional study of 298 street vendors in Chennai (65% women) found lower peak expiratory flow with more years of vending and high rates of cough at work (58.7%) and morning phlegm (44%); long-term exposure metrics were stronger predictors than short-term ones.
notes: Exposure measured with AQI, not personal monitoring; association only

claim: A 2026 CHI paper examines how pollution information and closures affect marginalised livelihoods in India; its findings could not be read for this edition.
notes: Identified only; abstract not accessible

Bank DBS Indonesia announced on 20 August 2024 a partnership with Nafas to install 50 air quality sensors, as part of the grant Nafas received through the DBS Foundation Business for Impact Grant Award 2023.

Clean Air Fund lists a 2023 grant to IIT Delhi to generate localised evidence on the health and climate impacts of air pollution.

Clean Air Fund lists a 2023 grant to World Resources Institute to support the city administrations of Agra and Gorakhpur (Uttar Pradesh) under the 'Accelerator for Clean Air Actions' across 10 Indian cities.
Clean Air Fund lists grants to the Confederation of Indian Industry for the India CEO Forum for Clean Air (2019 and Phase 2 in 2023), a platform for industry leaders on air pollution.

Clean Air Fund lists a 2023 grant to TERI for a strategic and policy advisory unit giving technical assistance to the Uttar Pradesh Clean Air Management Programme (UP CAMP).

Clean Air Fund lists grants to IIT Kanpur for an AI-based decision support system for Lucknow (2021), the ATMAN Centre of Excellence and a core support grant (2023).
Clean Air Fund lists a 2022 grant to ICCT for the TRUE Initiative in India, assessing real-world emissions of Delhi's vehicle fleet.

Clean Air Fund lists 2021 grants in Delhi to ICLEI (city leadership with NCR urban local bodies), Pravah (youth in urban slums, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh), Clean Air Asia (MSME air pollution learnings), Sesame Workshop India (children's voices) and Swaniti (policy support for Delhi and Uttar Pradesh).

Clean Air Fund lists grants to Health Care Without Harm in 2019 (positioning India's health sector on air pollution) and 2023 (health professionals working with governments in Delhi, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh), and names its partner programme 'Doctors For Clean Air'.
Clean Air Fund lists 2024 grants to Vital Strategies (implementing Breathe Cities in Jakarta) and C40 Cities (extended support to build Jakarta's planned Clean Air Zone).

EPIC's 2025 award to PAQI supports 70 affordable PM2.5 monitors installed with the National Emergencies Operation Center of Pakistan's National Disaster Management Authority, to support the National Clean Air Policy.
EPIC's 2025 award to Clean Energy Nepal supports 21 low-cost monitors in major Nepali cities with government partners, open data and youth trained to share it.
EPIC's 2025 award to Green Decision Labs and Research supports 40 low-cost monitors to identify the schools in Kathmandu Valley most affected by poor air quality.
EPIC's 2025 award to The Urban Unit supports 160 low-cost monitors across 10 Pakistani cities with data published on an open portal and health advisories.
EPIC's 2025 award to the University of the Punjab supports Faisalabad's first air quality monitoring network of 10 low-cost monitors across industrial, commercial and residential areas.
EPIC's 2025 award to Sherubtse College supports low-cost PM2.5 monitors at 15 locations across Bhutan, with a counterpart in the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources.

EPIC's 2026 award to Smart Air Bangladesh supports monitors around Dhaka's Matuail and Aminbazar landfills to measure the contribution of waste burning, working with BRAC Institute of Governance and Development and the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association.
EPIC's 2026 award to OBHIZATRIK Foundation supports 'Breathing Dhaka', placing sensors in informal settlements, industrial zones and dense residential areas and publishing readings live.

EPIC's 2026 award to Universiti Putra Malaysia and GO AQS supports 'AIRCHAMP', generating evidence to identify at-risk communities and strengthen Malaysia's Clean Air Action Plan.

EPIC's 2026 award to the Ateneo School of Medicine and Public Health supports Cebu City's first high-density low-cost sensor network with the Cebu City Government, public health warnings and work towards a local air quality ordinance.

Clean Up Nepal's 'Breathing Easier' project, funded by the EPIC Air Quality Fund with Green Decision Labs as consortium partner from 1 February 2025, reports 40 PM2.5 sensors in Kathmandu schools, open data via OpenAQ and awareness sessions for 1,500 students and 80 teachers.
notes: Outputs organisation-reported

claim: Clean Energy Nepal's Swachh Hawa Pariyojana plans 12 months of community PM2.5 measurement with municipalities in 10 cities across all seven provinces, a Nepali-language dashboard and support to national and local air quality plans.

ICIMOD, the Federation of Nepal Brick Industries and MinErgy jointly launched a design manual for rebuilding brick kilns as improved zigzag kilns after the 2015 earthquake; ICIMOD's director general said the design could cut coal use by up to 30%.
notes: The 30% figure is a stated potential, not a measured result

claim: In February 2018 ICIMOD convened brick manufacturers from Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Pakistan in Kathmandu to exchange zigzag kiln design and construction practice.

PAQI describes itself as an independent research organisation providing open data, scientific analysis and technical support for air quality management in Pakistan since 2016, and publishes weekly city briefs.
PAQI's November 2026 crop-burning report found Lahore averaged 175 µg/m³ of PM2.5 on days its air had passed over active burning, against 93 µg/m³ on other days.
In November 2020 the High Court declared a Jashore brick kiln's operations illegal and ordered it shut, disposing of a writ petition filed by the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association.

Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh filed a writ on Dhaka's air pollution in January 2019; the High Court ordered the Department of Environment to run mobile court drives twice a week against polluters.
Stamford University's Center for Atmospheric Pollution Studies (CAPS) reported that Dhaka had acceptable air on only 38 days between 2016 and 2021.

Purpose reports that it worked with the IKEA Foundation and Clean Air Fund to develop Help Delhi Breathe, a coalition campaign begun in 2015, and gave an innovation micro-grant for its first materials.
notes: Outcomes listed on the page are Purpose's attributions, not shown here

claim: Mahila Housing Trust and Help Delhi Breathe train women from Delhi's unrecognised settlements as 'AQI ambassadors' who carry portable monitors; Help Delhi Breathe also works with Bucketlist and the Centre for Social Equity and Inclusion on door-to-door drives.
Warrior Moms, co-founded in 2020 by Bhavreen Kandhari, is a network of mothers across India campaigning for clean air and climate action for their children.
From December 2017 Respirer Living Sciences, IIT Kanpur and Shakti Sustainable Energy Foundation built a sensor-based PM2.5 and PM10 network across 10 Indian cities using Respirer's Atmos devices.
Oizom, an Ahmedabad-based monitoring company, announced in April 2022 that it had set up 129 air quality monitors across nine Indian smart cities, including Bhagalpur in Bihar.
notes: Company-reported

claim: Airveda states that it is an approved vendor for construction-site air quality monitoring to the Delhi Pollution Control Committee and several Maharashtra municipal corporations, where rules require sites to monitor and share data.
notes: Company-reported

claim: Aurassure markets environmental and air quality monitoring for cities and renewable-energy sites.
notes: Company-reported

claim: CSTEP set up the India Sensor Evaluation and Training (Indi-SET) facility in Bengaluru in December 2023 for independent testing, calibration and training on low-cost sensors.

CSTEP's April 2026 evaluation co-located 48 multi-pollutant sensor devices from six manufacturers (Aeron, Airveda, Airvoice, Aurassure, Respirer, Sensit) with a reference monitor for up to eight months; none of the manufacturers met precision targets for nitrogen dioxide and ozone.
locator: Press release; annexure contents; news report

claim: Bicara Udara is a non-profit that advocates for clean-air policy, running an ambassadors programme (Biru Voices), a discussion platform (Biru Talks) and a schools alliance (Biru School Alliance).

Nafas Indonesia states that it operates the largest air quality sensor network in Greater Jakarta, with more than 100 outdoor sensors built with the European sensor company Airly and calibrated against local reference stations.
notes: Company-reported

claim: Nafas Foundation describes itself as a non-profit initiative of Nafas Indonesia, and says the network has grown to more than 219 sensors across 23 cities and is now 'powered by the Nafas Foundation'.
notes: Organisation-reported

claim: Nafas reported in September 2024 that it had installed 19 of the 50 DBS Foundation-supported sensors across 14 Indonesian cities.
notes: Organisation-reported

claim: A July 2025 white paper by Nafas, DBS Foundation and the University of Indonesia's Faculty of Public Health reports that a 10 µg/m³ rise in PM2.5 was associated with a twofold rise in pneumonia prevalence among under-fives in several Jakarta sub-districts.
notes: White paper; association only; not peer reviewed

claim: On 16 September 2021 the Central Jakarta District Court ruled for the Citizens' Lawsuit on Jakarta Air Pollution, finding seven state officials negligent, including the President and three governors.
On 13 November 2023 the Supreme Court rejected the government's cassation appeal; Koalisi Ibukota, the citizens' coalition behind the lawsuit, urged the government to implement the ruling.
notes: Implementation of the ruling not established in sources read

claim: Thailand Clean Air Network describes itself as a group of citizen volunteers and academics working with public, private and civil-society actors for clean air in Thailand.
One of seven Clean Air Act drafts approved by Thailand's cabinet on 28 November 2023 was proposed by Thailand Clean Air Network.

Thailand's House passed the Clean Air Bill 309-0 on 21 October 2025; in September 2026 the House rejected the Senate's amendments 414-2, sending the bill to a 20-member joint committee. No source read shows it enacted by the cutoff.
The Chiang Mai Breath Council was established in 2019 by public-health, private-sector and civil-society organisations as a mechanism for tackling Chiang Mai's air pollution.
More than 1,700 plaintiffs filed a lawsuit at the Chiang Mai Administrative Court on 10 April 2023 against the Prime Minister and national bodies for failing to address seasonal haze.

Live & Learn Vietnam reports that its Building Green Schools for a Green Hanoi programme, piloted in 2021, involved more than 69 schools in four districts and scaled to all 93 schools in Dong Anh district, supported by the USAID-funded CAfCA project with Hanoi's environment and education departments.
notes: Organisation-reported; no air-quality outcome reported

claim: Winrock International led the USAID Reducing Pollution project in Viet Nam, working on open burning of waste and straw, craft-village emissions (including aluminium recycling at Binh Yen with VESDI) and a roadmap for vehicle emission regulations.

The GEF records project 10609 (e-mobility in the Philippines) with UNIDO as implementing agency and the Department of Trade and Industry as executing agency, approved for implementation on 1 July 2022 with a GEF grant of US$3,788,990 and US$77,477,969 of co-financing.

UNIDO enlisted a consortium of Clean Air Asia, De La Salle University, the Electric Vehicle Association of the Philippines and the Urban Electric Mobility Initiative for E-Mobility ASAP, which focuses on electric public utility vehicles, electric two-wheelers, batteries and electronics.
Health Care Without Harm Southeast Asia and 350 Pilipinas organised a Walk for Clean Air in Quezon City on 7 December 2025 with more than 500 participants, calling for updated air quality standards.
The ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control was soft-launched on 5 September 2023 at the 43rd ASEAN Summit hosted by Indonesia.
CREA is an independent research organisation registered as a non-profit in Finland, with staff across Asia and Europe, funded by philanthropic grants and commissioned research.
OpenAQ is a non-profit that aggregates and harmonises open air quality data on an open-access platform.

TERI-ARAI attribute Delhi-NCR's much higher winter concentrations to adverse meteorology: lower wind speed and a lower boundary layer reduce the atmosphere's capacity to disperse pollution, raising concentrations near the ground.
notes: systems-map edition: atmosphere layer

claim: The World Bank's Nepal report states that biomass-fuelled household stoves create both indoor and ambient (outdoor) air pollution.
notes: systems-map edition: household fuel to ambient link

claim: The World Bank describes an airshed as a region sharing a common flow of air that can extend over several hundred kilometres, beyond city and state boundaries, which makes air pollution multi-sectoral and multi-jurisdictional.
notes: systems-map edition: shared airsheds

claim: A 2019 modelling study estimates that removing all household emissions (biomass for cooking and heating, kerosene for lighting) would lower India's population-weighted annual ambient PM2.5 from 55.1 to 38 µg/m³ against a 2015 baseline, meeting the national standard on average, while highly polluted areas such as Delhi would stay above it.
notes: systems-map edition: household emissions contribute to outdoor air
